results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The intro reader reconstructed all six roadmap stages in order (four drawings; steps, promise and handoff, entities, status lines; the walk; four message failures and checks; vendors and law; growth) and named vendor documentation and law as evidence.
Every outline summary matches the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph in order; the three intro callouts have no spec paragraph by design.
The outliner marked no unit as carrying two ideas.

Every unit serves a supporting claim: scene S1, steps and promises S2, handoffs and requirements S3, status lines S4, the walk S5, failures and remedies S6; public record and scale stages support S3, S4 and S6.

Each table is introduced and read (steps, entities, per-system knowledge, requirements, per-step failures); each figure has an explanatory caption; the statistics (24%, 70.22%, 18%) and the vendor and legal quotations are each tied to the point they support.

Every declared transition is carried at its boundary, e.g. 'A handoff is a message about something' (sequence), 'An order, then, is made of several things, and they do not move together' (additional support), 'Each of those failures missed a requirement' (cause-effect), 'Two ideas ... are the field's answer' (problem-solution), 'Kestrel & Pine is fictional; its handoffs are not' (additional support).

results.quote: This price, this variant, in stock, delivered by then
results.finding: 'Variant' (the SKU, on does_not_know) is used in the step-2 row of the steps table and only defined later, in the entity table of 'The Things an Order Is Made Of'.

results.quote: Invoice, credit note, matching the PSP's payouts (its transfers to the merchant) to orders, month-end
results.finding: 'Credit note' appears in the step-13 row of the steps table without a gloss, while the payout beside it is glossed; it is explained only later in the entity table, and a newcomer outside finance would not know it.

results.quote: **Where we are in the order's journey.** Eva Janssen buys a jacket and socks from Kestrel & Pine
results.finding: The label 'Where we are in the order's journey' in the book's first chapter confused both readers (we are nowhere in the journey yet), and Eva is then set aside for Noor's scene.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B: item 2, same label and the switch to Noor

results.quote: The table and the introduction have already used two words for that pairing, *promise* and *handoff*; this section defines them
results.finding: Promise was already defined before the steps table, so announcing that this section defines it sent both readers back to check; the spec's p14 controlling idea itself says the section defines both words.

results.quote: Kestrel & Pine's **Three-Status Order**, #1052877, shows what happens when even one line is flattened: the goods line of a two-parcel order, reduced to one word, which three systems then read three ways (a case of Schrödinger's Order).
results.finding: Both readers re-read this sentence and lost its link to the section's claim: the section argues three lines must not be merged into one status, but the declared example shows a partial shipment flattened within the goods line alone.

results.quote: The shop platform then showed *Delivered* after the carrier's scan.
results.finding: Reader A had to re-read to connect 'fulfilled' at the end of the previous sentence with 'Delivered' here, because the cause and its visible effect sit in separate sentences without a link.

results.quote: **Step 13, accounting (the ERP).** Accounting began at dispatch: on Wednesday 14 April
results.finding: After step 12 reached 22 April, step 13 jumps back to 14 April and forward again; both readers had to reorient. The spec's flow rationale declares this placement (accounting told last).
results.corroborated_by: flow-B: item 8, same jump back to 14 April

results.draft_locus: Why the Joins Are Where Things Break ¶6
results.quote: Each of those failures missed a requirement the business sets for a handoff, usually without saying so
results.finding: With the requirements paragraph and its table placed between the four failures and the remedies, reader A had to look back up a table to see what idempotency and reconciliation answer; the spec declares this order.

results.quote: With those it follows one order through the systems that hold it, shows the four ways the messages between them fail and the checks that let a merchant explain what happened, sets that account against what vendors and the law document, and ends with what changes as a merchant grows.
results.finding: Reader B had to re-read the roadmap: five chained clauses in one sentence, with 'the checks that let a merchant explain what happened' unclear on first reading.

results.quote: Storefront, payment provider, warehouse, carrier, returns portal and finance system each hold their own copy of the order or of their part of it.
results.finding: Reader B paused to check whether this list of six matched the body's seven systems, because the callout names them differently (storefront, finance system) from the body (shop platform, ERP).

results.quote: Three things about the table matter before any technology is named.
results.finding: Reader B re-read this sentence because the previous section had already named the shop platform, PSP, WMS, ERP, PostNL, returns portal and iPaaS, so 'before any technology is named' did not fit.

results.quote: The goods line alone, for a simple order, looks like this:
results.finding: Only the goods line's states are shown; the money and returns lines are named but never given states, so reader B had nothing concrete to map Shopify's and commercetools' payment and return states onto later. The spec's section flow declares only the goods line drawn.

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong at Each Step ¶1
results.quote: Payment succeeded but no order was created (the shopper closed the tab)
results.finding: Reader B read this row as contradicting the walk, which had just said the shop platform creates the order with payment pending before the result arrives; the row does not say it describes platforms that create the order only after payment.
The introduction opens on a concrete example (pick list, invoice and service ticket disagreeing while the shopper waits), not a placeholder, definition or sweeping opener.
The conclusion sorts the chapter's claims into established, context-dependent and the author's synthesis, then gives questions and the hand-off; no weak pattern found.

The synthesis ('judge an architecture by its handoffs, not by its boxes') and the so-what ('the table of what each system knows at each moment is the cheapest architecture document a merchant can produce') are both stated.

It calls back to the four drawings: 'I follow one real order ... as Noor did' and the first question, 'Can someone draw the order's path through every system, with the message that carries each handoff and the person who owns it?'
The reader named the warehouse-to-shop shipment handoff on the goods line (a misread partial shipment, the Three-Status Order), matching the expected answer.
The reader named a duplicated message (two senders, no shared record), reconciliation of returns against refunds to detect it, and idempotency so a repeated refund has no second effect.
